What We Do
Advance Transdisciplinary Climate Justice Research
SSL’s work integrates community knowledge and multiple disciplines, in deeply collaborative ways, to develop creative and sustainable approaches that center community and justice. We expand and rewrite what "counts" as climate research by pulling in experts from outside the natural sciences and fostering an inviting and diverse research community.
Convene for Networking and Field-Building
Through our convenings, workshops, and events, we create spaces for people to build relationships across boundaries, learn from each other, and work together.
Drive Equitable Climate Adaptation
We stand with communities historically and currently excluded from political power and economic resources. Our work is not just about documenting damage, but about truly listening and exploring desired futures together. Through our research, events, and initiatives, we collaborate with others to move the region toward equitable adaptation.
What I value so much about my work with SSL is the opportunity to be both expert and novice. With the Northeast Climate Justice Research Collaborative, my training and research are valued and there is space for my curiosity and further exploration. This has allowed me to pose questions bringing together climate change and racial justice in a way I never would have previously.”

Climate Careers Curricula Initiative (C3I)
The Climate Careers Curricula Initiative (C3 Initiative), supported by the Liberty Mutual Foundation (LMF), aims to create and offer microcredentialed training programs for blue and green jobs in Greater Boston. This comprehensive, community-centered approach focuses on providing career pathways for underrepresented populations, especially vulnerable young adults, people of color, and low-income adults from environmental justice communities. 

Key elements of the program will include:

Key elements of the program will include: 

Curriculum Development: Collaborating with industry partners, community-based organizations, and academic experts to develop microcredentialed training programs for high-demand blue and green jobs. 
Community Engagement: Recruiting participants from environmental justice communities by working closely with local organizations and city programs.
Partnerships for Career Pathways: Establishing partnerships with employers to create pathways from training to employment, including internships, job placement assistance, and mentoring. 
Continuous Evaluation: Regularly assessing program outcomes to ensure alignment with community needs and industry demands.
Greater Impact We will work with local and state policymakers to share our findings on addressing systemic barriers to entry in blue and green jobs. 
The initiative plans to develop six microcredentialed programs over three years, covering areas such as solar installation, energy auditing, and nature-based solutions. The program aims to enroll 90 participants over 3 years, with 75% of participants coming from underrepresented groups.

Climate Inequality and Integrative Resilience (CLIIR) Initiative
With climate resilience and inequality as an umbrella, the CLIIR Initiative focuses on three main themes: Indigenous Knowledge and Governance, Climate Migration, and Climate Change and Health. Our work was funded by a National Science Foundation planning grant through the Centers for Research Innovation in Science, Environment, and Society (CRISES) program. 

We work with these three themes because they: 

leverage areas of strength within our team and partner networks. 
have significant interconnections, fostering our capacity to think and work holistically.  
provide testing grounds for building the Decision Support Hub and advancing the study of individual and collective decision-making.

Cape Cod Rail Resilience Project
The Sustainable Solutions Lab (SSL) is proud to be part of the Cape Cod Rail Resilience Project, led by Carlos Velásquez, a PhD candidate at UMass Boston and project manager at MassDOT.
This initiative aims to improve rail safety and climate resilience along the Cape Main Line by integrating advanced technology with stakeholder-driven research methods. The project, inspired by Velásquez’s doctoral research, addresses the increasing risks posed by climate change to critical transportation infrastructure. It was launched in response to a significant 300-foot rail embankment collapse in East Sandwich in 2020, an event linked to climate change-induced drought conditions. With USDOT funding, the team is using drones for mapping and sensors for monitoring water levels. This collaborative effort brings together MassDOT, UMass Boston, and AECOM experts. The innovative approach combines aerial surveys, hydrological drought analysis, and real-time monitoring systems at three pilot study sites.

Climate Inequality and Integrative Resilience (CLIIR) Initiative
With climate resilience and inequality as an umbrella, the CLIIR Initiative focuses on three main themes: Indigenous Knowledge and Governance, Climate Migration, and Climate Change and Health. Our work was funded by a National Science Foundation planning grant through the Centers for Research Innovation in Science, Environment, and Society (CRISES) program. 

We work with these three themes because they: 

leverage areas of strength within our team and partner networks. 
have significant interconnections, fostering our capacity to think and work holistically.  
provide testing grounds for building the Decision Support Hub and advancing the study of individual and collective decision-making.

Launched in the Spring of 2022, the Northeast Climate Justice Research Collaborative (The Collaborative) is a trans-disciplinary network for academic and community researchers in the Northeast.

The Collaborative is composed of researchers—whether experienced or just getting started—who are interested in actively working to advance practices and policies that ensure historically excluded communities are safe and healthy despite the changing climate. Through networking, dialogue, funding, and resource-sharing, we support scholars to maximize the benefits of research for the communities they are working with. The Collaborative is convened by the Sustainable Solutions Lab (SSL) at UMass Boston.

WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

INVESTING IN FACULTY

SLIDE 18 — INVESTING IN FACULTY
================================================================================
Faculty and students are the foundation of everything SSL does. Through research
funding and professional development, SSL can ensure that those who are best
positioned to bring new approaches and shift the field can do so. SSL's approach
is to support faculty's research and their development as scholars, as they are
essential to generating the evidence and advocacy needed for equitable adaptation.
In support of these goals, we created a semester-long program on climate justice
for faculty, built a climate justice research database and granted research and
seed grants.
================================================================================

of climate change across racial groups in the Boston area and intentionally
including a large sampling of people of color. The report is released in
partnership with the Barr Foundation.
HEAR FROM THE AUTHORS:
"I think it is incredibly important for our voices to be in the table. Most of
the local and national studies on climate change done to date have only been
including the voices and the experiences of the white population."
— Lorna Rivera, Mauricio Gaston Institute for Latino Community
"We hear a lot of speculation about what communities of color might or might not
think about climate change, but we thought it was important to actually ask them."
— Rosalyn Negron, Associate Professor of Anthropology
"We need data that reflects everyone in society, especially significant and
long-silenced communities, if we want equitable climate change policies and
responses."
— J. Cedric Woods, Institute for New England Native American Studies
KEY FINDINGS:
- Residents of color are more likely than white residents to believe that
climate change is happening in Massachusetts (8 in 10) and is a very
serious threat.
- White respondents are the least inclined to view climate change impacts as
affecting some people more than others.
- Respondents, regardless of race, overwhelmingly agree that combatting
climate change requires "major" steps at the federal and state levels.

Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.

communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

Committee (JSC). This is the first time since WCRP was established in 1980 that
it made a membership call specifically for social and economic scientists as part
of its new strategic plan. Professor Ivanova was selected from over 130 applicants
to join the 18-person committee.

In December, the Sustainable Solutions Lab hosted a virtual conversation that
spotlighted renowned leaders in the climate adaptation field who contributed to
the new anthology ALL WE CAN SAVE. The book illuminates the need for
transformational climate leadership that is more characteristically feminine and
more faithfully feminist and rooted in compassion, connection, creativity, and
collaboration.
Panelists included co-editor Katharine K. Wilkinson and contributors Colette
Pichon Battle, Jainey K. Bavishi, and Susanne C. Moser. Nationally-syndicated
radio show Living on Earth co-sponsored the event, with Steve Curwood serving
as moderator.

Katsyris Rivera Kientz is a Sociology PhD candidate at UMass Boston. She graduated from the University of Puerto Rico in Cayey and completed her Master at UMB’s Transnational, Cultural and Community Studies program. Her research interests lie at the intersection of Political Sociology; Transnational activism; Colonialism; National Identity; Education; Race and gender issues; Natural and not-so-natural disasters, and the Puerto Rico-United States political relationship. PORTABLE MEMORIES IN RISING SEAS

SLIDE 43 — PORTABLE MEMORIES IN RISING SEAS
================================================================================
This event, cohosted by the Climigration Network and featuring the Fifty-Fifty
art collective's multimedia project Portable Memories in Rising Seas, was an
opportunity to reflect on our relationships to the places we call home in the
context of climate change and sea level rise.
After watching short videos of communities facing relocation due to rising sea
levels, attendees grappled with the implications of climate change as they
manifest on individual and collective levels through drawings and group discussion.
The Fifty-Fifty art collective encouraged participants to explore questions such as:
- How are you affected by the climate crisis?
- How is your relationship to the place you call home changing as the planet warms?
- How can we transform our grief about climate change into action?
Following the event, participants' drawings were turned into prints that become an
archive of our memories and concerns. These may help us to remember our
communities before the hurricanes, fires and rising seas in the future.
================================================================================

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY

SLIDE 5 — CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================
The first of UMass Boston's Campus Goals for the academic year 2020-21 is to
make UMass Boston a leading anti-racist, health promoting public research
university with excellence at its core. SSL's core values align with this goal.
The below definitions are key to understanding our work:
CLIMATE CHANGE
A shift in average global weather patterns due to increased greenhouse gas
emissions in the atmosphere. It disproportionately impacts low-income
communities and communities of color.
SYSTEMIC RACISM
Among other injustices, systemic racism causes these communities to suffer
more pollution, failing infrastructure, and increased exposure to climate risks.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION
Focused on better protecting people, homes and communities from the impacts
of the climate crisis.
CLIMATE JUSTICE
Climate action that recognizes past injustices and moves us closer to a world
where everyone can thrive despite a changing climate.
================================================================================

WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

DIRECTOR'S MESSAGE

SLIDE 3 — DIRECTOR'S MESSAGE
================================================================================
2020 strengthened our resolve to pursue climate justice.
The disproportionate impacts of Covid-19, the increased awakening around racial
justice and the near constant barrage of climate disasters made it clear that
SSL's work is essential and that there are many opportunities for us to lead.
I have been buoyed by how much the national conversation has changed around
climate change and systemic racism over the last year. The Sustainable Solutions
Lab is working to ensure that our climate adaptation efforts take into account
historic marginalization and the disproportionate impact on vulnerable communities.
The climate justice research we are doing, along with showing up for our faculty
of color and community partners, are critical for dismantling white supremacy in
climate adaptation work.
We will secure a safe and healthy future for everyone in the face of the climate
crisis.
With hope,
Rebecca Herst
Director, Sustainable Solutions Lab
================================================================================

CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY

SLIDE 5 — CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================
The first of UMass Boston's Campus Goals for the academic year 2020-21 is to
make UMass Boston a leading anti-racist, health promoting public research
university with excellence at its core. SSL's core values align with this goal.
The below definitions are key to understanding our work:
CLIMATE CHANGE
A shift in average global weather patterns due to increased greenhouse gas
emissions in the atmosphere. It disproportionately impacts low-income
communities and communities of color.
SYSTEMIC RACISM
Among other injustices, systemic racism causes these communities to suffer
more pollution, failing infrastructure, and increased exposure to climate risks.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION
Focused on better protecting people, homes and communities from the impacts
of the climate crisis.
CLIMATE JUSTICE
Climate action that recognizes past injustices and moves us closer to a world
where everyone can thrive despite a changing climate.
================================================================================

SPECIAL EVENTS: ALL WE CAN SAVE

SLIDE 41 — SPECIAL EVENTS: ALL WE CAN SAVE
================================================================================
A number of special climate change events were hosted by SSL faculty in 2020-21
from All We Can Save to the celebration of Indigenous People's Day with a
discussion on "Climate Change and Indigenous Resistance: An Intergenerational and
Inter-Tribal Conversation" to ART EVENTS.
ALL WE CAN SAVE: Truth, Courage, and Solutions for the Climate Crisis
In December, the Sustainable Solutions Lab hosted a virtual conversation that
spotlighted renowned leaders in the climate adaptation field who contributed to
the new anthology ALL WE CAN SAVE. The book illuminates the need for
transformational climate leadership that is more characteristically feminine and
more faithfully feminist and rooted in compassion, connection, creativity, and
collaboration.
Panelists included co-editor Katharine K. Wilkinson and contributors Colette
Pichon Battle, Jainey K. Bavishi, and Susanne C. Moser. Nationally-syndicated
radio show Living on Earth co-sponsored the event, with Steve Curwood serving
as moderator.
================================================================================

SLIDE 46 — SUPPORT SSL / SUPPORT CLIMATE JUSTICE
================================================================================
To move forward on equitable climate solutions, we need everyone.
Nearly 100% of our funding comes from external sources.
And nearly 100% goes directly into climate justice research.
Your investment means:
- Deeper relationships on the ground in Boston so we can stand in solidarity
with the city
- A coordinated, cross-disciplinary research agenda developed in partnership
with frontline communities and policymakers
- Research funds for junior BIPOC faculty to bring new approaches to equitable
adaptation
Give today!
================================================================================

SLIDE 20 — CLIMATE JUSTICE DEEP DIVE
================================================================================
To seed additional climate justice collaborations on campus, the Sustainable
Solutions Lab hosted a fall semester program for faculty, called the Climate
Justice Deep Dive, created with Climate Justice expert and consultant Karla
Tandon. 20 faculty from schools and institutes across UMass Boston engaged with
current research and trends in climate justice, fostering connections and
relationships within the group, and deepening their capacity to address climate
justice in their scholarship. The Committee included guest lectures on climate
justice topics from scholars and practitioners in the field. Guest speakers
included Zakeem Adris and Dina Gilio-Whitaker.
PARTICIPANT EXPERIENCE:
"[A] truly unique and inspiring experience... [The Climate Justice Deep Dive]
emboldened me to gather seemingly disparate parts of my research together to
take it in a new and much more meaningful direction."
Brian Halley @brianhalley, Oct 16, 2020:
"Just have to applaud an amazing 'Climate Justice Deep Dive' group at
@UMassBoston where I get to Zoom with brilliant faculty and discuss environmental
racism and climate and white supremacy in a tangible and fascinating way, every
two weeks, woman guests & readings."

CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE

SLIDE 24 — CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE
================================================================================
Many SSL faculty are relatively new to the field of climate justice. To help them
ground their own scholarship in the academic conversation, Rosalyn Negron and
graduate student Katsyris Rivera-Kientz have created a database of climate justice
research articles. All research starts with a literature review. Launched in March
2021, this resource (housed in Mendeley) contains over 500 articles in a wide
variety of topics from health to housing to governance. All SSL faculty have
access to it and are able to contribute to it themselves so that it will continue
to evolve as expertise on campus grows. This is a central, living resource for SSL
faculty to begin their exploration of climate justice topics.
"Having access to the climate justice research database has allowed me to very
quickly get up to speed on where the academic conversations are in fields beyond
my own. It's giving me a broader interdisciplinary perspective that is essential
for the directions I want to take my research."
— Antonio Raciti, Assistant Professor of Ecological Design, School for the Environment
================================================================================

INVESTING IN FACULTY

SLIDE 18 — INVESTING IN FACULTY
================================================================================
Faculty and students are the foundation of everything SSL does. Through research
funding and professional development, SSL can ensure that those who are best
positioned to bring new approaches and shift the field can do so. SSL's approach
is to support faculty's research and their development as scholars, as they are
essential to generating the evidence and advocacy needed for equitable adaptation.
In support of these goals, we created a semester-long program on climate justice
for faculty, built a climate justice research database and granted research and
seed grants.
================================================================================

BARR FOUNDATION AWARDS ADDITIONAL FUNDS TO SUPPORT FACULTY OF COLOR

SLIDE 31 — BARR FOUNDATION AWARDS ADDITIONAL FUNDS TO SUPPORT FACULTY OF COLOR
================================================================================
SSL received $20,000 from the Barr Foundation to deepen our commitment to
centering Racial Justice in our work and support our efforts to be an anti-racist
research institute at UMB. As part of this effort, SSL provided Summer
Anti-Racism Research Funding to seven projects led by affiliated faculty with
grants of up to $2,500 for climate justice research that do at least one of
the following:
- Identify disproportionate impacts of climate change on different racial groups
- Propose anti-racist policy changes to address climate disparities
- Center BIPOC voices in the research efforts
================================================================================

HEAR FROM THE AUTHORS:

the local and national studies on climate change done to date have only been
including the voices and the experiences of the white population."
— Lorna Rivera, Mauricio Gaston Institute for Latino Community
"We hear a lot of speculation about what communities of color might or might not

long-silenced communities, if we want equitable climate change policies and
responses."

KEY FINDINGS:
- Residents of color are more likely than white residents to believe that
climate change is happening in Massachusetts (8 in 10) and is a very
serious threat.
- White respondents are the least inclined to view climate change impacts as
affecting some people more than others.
- Respondents, regardless of race, overwhelmingly agree that combatting
climate change requires "major" steps at the federal and state levels.

SLIDE 10 — RESEARCH
================================================================================
Without climate justice research designed and conducted in partnership with
marginalized communities, adaptation efforts may exacerbate existing inequities
and negatively impact society's resilience as a whole.
SSL is stitching these previously siloed areas of expertise into an
interdisciplinary approach and fostering new relationships across fields in order
to better address these extremely complex and interconnected challenges and
catalyze change.
================================================================================
SLIDES 11-12 — VIEWS THAT MATTER: RACE AND OPINIONS ON CLIMATE CHANGE
OF BOSTON AREA RESIDENTS
================================================================================
A growing body of research finds that climate change places a disproportionate
burden on communities of color in the United States. In spite of this evidence,
important discussions taking place about climate change — such as how it is
experienced, which policy solutions are most critical and how we can prepare for
and adapt to its impacts — often leave out the voices of the very communities
most affected.

of climate change across racial groups in the Boston area and intentionally

Climate Adaptation Forum
 
The Climate Adaptation Forum is a quarterly series of half-day events organized 
by the Environmental Business Council and the Sustainable Solutions Lab at 
the University of Massachusetts Boston. These forums provide cutting-edge 
thought leadership on adaptation to climate change for environmental and 
energy professionals, policymakers, municipal officials, NGOs, and practitioners.
 
Starting in 2017, these forums have been addressing a broad array of topics 
through local, national, and global speakers representing forward-thinking  
institutions, global firms, academia, government, and more. They provide a  
regular, ongoing opportunity for adaptation professionals from various fields 
in the Boston area to meet and cross-pollinate ideas and share solutions to 
common problems.

Without climate justice research designed and conducted in partnership with
marginalized communities, adaptation efforts may exacerbate existing inequities
and negatively impact society's resilience as a whole.
SSL is stitching these previously siloed areas of expertise into an
interdisciplinary approach and fostering new relationships across fields in order
to better address these extremely complex and interconnected challenges and
catalyze change.

OF BOSTON AREA RESIDENTS

A growing body of research finds that climate change places a disproportionate
burden on communities of color in the United States. In spite of this evidence,
important discussions taking place about climate change — such as how it is
experienced, which policy solutions are most critical and how we can prepare for
and adapt to its impacts — often leave out the voices of the very communities
most affected.

- Propose anti-racist policy changes to address climate disparities
- Center BIPOC voices in the research efforts
================================================================================

SLIDE 20 — CLIMATE JUSTICE DEEP DIVE
================================================================================
To seed additional climate justice collaborations on campus, the Sustainable
Solutions Lab hosted a fall semester program for faculty, called the Climate
Justice Deep Dive, created with Climate Justice expert and consultant Karla
Tandon. 20 faculty from schools and institutes across UMass Boston engaged with
current research and trends in climate justice, fostering connections and
relationships within the group, and deepening their capacity to address climate
justice in their scholarship. The Committee included guest lectures on climate
justice topics from scholars and practitioners in the field. Guest speakers
included Zakeem Adris and Dina Gilio-Whitaker.
PARTICIPANT EXPERIENCE:
"[A] truly unique and inspiring experience... [The Climate Justice Deep Dive]
emboldened me to gather seemingly disparate parts of my research together to
take it in a new and much more meaningful direction."

"Just have to applaud an amazing 'Climate Justice Deep Dive' group at
@UMassBoston where I get to Zoom with brilliant faculty and discuss environmental
racism and climate and white supremacy in a tangible and fascinating way, every
two weeks, woman guests & readings."

PORTABLE MEMORIES IN RISING SEAS

SLIDE 43 — PORTABLE MEMORIES IN RISING SEAS
================================================================================
This event, cohosted by the Climigration Network and featuring the Fifty-Fifty
art collective's multimedia project Portable Memories in Rising Seas, was an
opportunity to reflect on our relationships to the places we call home in the
context of climate change and sea level rise.
After watching short videos of communities facing relocation due to rising sea
levels, attendees grappled with the implications of climate change as they
manifest on individual and collective levels through drawings and group discussion.
The Fifty-Fifty art collective encouraged participants to explore questions such as:
- How are you affected by the climate crisis?
- How is your relationship to the place you call home changing as the planet warms?
- How can we transform our grief about climate change into action?
Following the event, participants' drawings were turned into prints that become an
archive of our memories and concerns. These may help us to remember our
communities before the hurricanes, fires and rising seas in the future.
================================================================================

WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

it made a membership call specifically for social and economic scientists as part
of its new strategic plan. Professor Ivanova was selected from over 130 applicants
to join the 18-person committee.

LORENA ESTRADA-MARTINEZ RECEIVED $800K EPA GRANT
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) awarded Lorena Estrada-Martinez,
assistant professor of environment and public health in the School for the
Environment, a three-year grant of $800,000 to study health risks in Vieques,
Puerto Rico. As a result of contamination created by decades of U.S. military
occupation (including the use of chemical and biological weapons), the ecological
and human populations of Vieques have been significantly impacted.
Her study, "Community Driven Assessment of Environmental Health Risks in Vieques,
Puerto Rico," will be supported by a partnership between her research team and the
local community so that all are equally involved in decision-making and
knowledge-sharing. Her team includes SSL faculty members Bob Chen, interim dean
of the SFE and professor of organic geochemistry; Rosalyn Negron, associate
professor of anthropology in the College of Liberal Arts; and Lorna Rivera,
director of the Mauricio Gaston Institute for Latino Community Development and
Public Policy.

CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE

SLIDE 24 — CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE
================================================================================
Many SSL faculty are relatively new to the field of climate justice. To help them
ground their own scholarship in the academic conversation, Rosalyn Negron and
graduate student Katsyris Rivera-Kientz have created a database of climate justice
research articles. All research starts with a literature review. Launched in March
2021, this resource (housed in Mendeley) contains over 500 articles in a wide
variety of topics from health to housing to governance. All SSL faculty have
access to it and are able to contribute to it themselves so that it will continue
to evolve as expertise on campus grows. This is a central, living resource for SSL
faculty to begin their exploration of climate justice topics.
"Having access to the climate justice research database has allowed me to very
quickly get up to speed on where the academic conversations are in fields beyond
my own. It's giving me a broader interdisciplinary perspective that is essential
for the directions I want to take my research."
— Antonio Raciti, Assistant Professor of Ecological Design, School for the Environment
================================================================================

CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY

SLIDE 5 — CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================
The first of UMass Boston's Campus Goals for the academic year 2020-21 is to
make UMass Boston a leading anti-racist, health promoting public research
university with excellence at its core. SSL's core values align with this goal.
The below definitions are key to understanding our work:
CLIMATE CHANGE
A shift in average global weather patterns due to increased greenhouse gas
emissions in the atmosphere. It disproportionately impacts low-income
communities and communities of color.
SYSTEMIC RACISM
Among other injustices, systemic racism causes these communities to suffer
more pollution, failing infrastructure, and increased exposure to climate risks.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION
Focused on better protecting people, homes and communities from the impacts
of the climate crisis.
CLIMATE JUSTICE
Climate action that recognizes past injustices and moves us closer to a world
where everyone can thrive despite a changing climate.
================================================================================

DIRECTOR'S MESSAGE

SLIDE 3 — DIRECTOR'S MESSAGE
================================================================================
2020 strengthened our resolve to pursue climate justice.
The disproportionate impacts of Covid-19, the increased awakening around racial
justice and the near constant barrage of climate disasters made it clear that
SSL's work is essential and that there are many opportunities for us to lead.
I have been buoyed by how much the national conversation has changed around
climate change and systemic racism over the last year. The Sustainable Solutions
Lab is working to ensure that our climate adaptation efforts take into account
historic marginalization and the disproportionate impact on vulnerable communities.
The climate justice research we are doing, along with showing up for our faculty
of color and community partners, are critical for dismantling white supremacy in
climate adaptation work.
We will secure a safe and healthy future for everyone in the face of the climate
crisis.
With hope,
Rebecca Herst
Director, Sustainable Solutions Lab
================================================================================

SSL CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH GRANTS FOR FACULTY
In 2021, SSL awarded two research grants to support faculty conducting research
focused on climate justice. These grants, for up to $50,000, were open to
interdisciplinary teams of tenure or non-tenure track faculty members affiliated
with the colleges, schools and institutes that make up SSL.
PROJECT: Novel Research in Climate Justice: Including Transient Populations
in Climate Resiliency
School for Environment (SFE) associate dean Ellen Douglas, assistant professor
Evan Stewart from the College of Liberal Arts and SFE PhD candidate Johnna
Flahive are using their $48,000 Research Grant for a project that will
characterize the current status and vulnerability of transient populations
(homeless citizens and seasonal international visa workers) within the context
of climate-related risks, focusing on Boston and Cape Cod, Massachusetts. There
are many climate resiliency efforts underway in Massachusetts; however, all
efforts to date have seemingly overlooked transient populations. Their aim is to
identify historical barriers to and future opportunities for involving transient
populations in climate resilience planning and policies.
Ellen Douglas — Associate Dean, Professor of Hydrology, School for the Environment

SLIDE 20 — CLIMATE JUSTICE DEEP DIVE
================================================================================
To seed additional climate justice collaborations on campus, the Sustainable
Solutions Lab hosted a fall semester program for faculty, called the Climate
Justice Deep Dive, created with Climate Justice expert and consultant Karla
Tandon. 20 faculty from schools and institutes across UMass Boston engaged with
current research and trends in climate justice, fostering connections and
relationships within the group, and deepening their capacity to address climate
justice in their scholarship. The Committee included guest lectures on climate
justice topics from scholars and practitioners in the field. Guest speakers
included Zakeem Adris and Dina Gilio-Whitaker.
PARTICIPANT EXPERIENCE:
"[A] truly unique and inspiring experience... [The Climate Justice Deep Dive]
emboldened me to gather seemingly disparate parts of my research together to
take it in a new and much more meaningful direction."

@UMassBoston where I get to Zoom with brilliant faculty and discuss environmental
racism and climate and white supremacy in a tangible and fascinating way, every
two weeks, woman guests & readings."

PORTABLE MEMORIES IN RISING SEAS

SLIDE 43 — PORTABLE MEMORIES IN RISING SEAS
================================================================================
This event, cohosted by the Climigration Network and featuring the Fifty-Fifty
art collective's multimedia project Portable Memories in Rising Seas, was an
opportunity to reflect on our relationships to the places we call home in the
context of climate change and sea level rise.
After watching short videos of communities facing relocation due to rising sea
levels, attendees grappled with the implications of climate change as they
manifest on individual and collective levels through drawings and group discussion.
The Fifty-Fifty art collective encouraged participants to explore questions such as:
- How are you affected by the climate crisis?
- How is your relationship to the place you call home changing as the planet warms?
- How can we transform our grief about climate change into action?
Following the event, participants' drawings were turned into prints that become an
archive of our memories and concerns. These may help us to remember our
communities before the hurricanes, fires and rising seas in the future.
================================================================================

SLIDE 42 — CLIMATE EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS: ART x CULTURAL RESILIENCE
================================================================================
The interconnected crises of climate change, ecological collapse, institutional
racism and economic inequality are expanding. When facing these challenges, the
focus is often placed on immediate crisis response and the built environment
without accounting for the underlying cultural causes. In May, we hosted an event
where the speakers held a conversation that explored the wisdom and beauty of
different cultures, cultural organizing and artistic expression in the development
of resilient and sustainable communities.
Speakers:
Erin Genia — Artist-in-Residence, City of Boston
Meghan Venable-Thomas — Cultural Resilience Program Director,
Enterprise Community Partners
Moderator:
Kim Szeto — Public Art Program Director, New England Foundation for the Arts
================================================================================

CLIMATE EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS: ART x CULTURAL RESILIENCE

SLIDE 42 — CLIMATE EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS: ART x CULTURAL RESILIENCE
================================================================================
The interconnected crises of climate change, ecological collapse, institutional
racism and economic inequality are expanding. When facing these challenges, the
focus is often placed on immediate crisis response and the built environment
without accounting for the underlying cultural causes. In May, we hosted an event
where the speakers held a conversation that explored the wisdom and beauty of
different cultures, cultural organizing and artistic expression in the development
of resilient and sustainable communities.
Speakers:
Erin Genia — Artist-in-Residence, City of Boston
Meghan Venable-Thomas — Cultural Resilience Program Director,
Enterprise Community Partners
Moderator:
Kim Szeto — Public Art Program Director, New England Foundation for the Arts
================================================================================

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

SLIDE 10 — RESEARCH
================================================================================
Without climate justice research designed and conducted in partnership with
marginalized communities, adaptation efforts may exacerbate existing inequities
and negatively impact society's resilience as a whole.
SSL is stitching these previously siloed areas of expertise into an
interdisciplinary approach and fostering new relationships across fields in order
to better address these extremely complex and interconnected challenges and
catalyze change.
================================================================================
SLIDES 11-12 — VIEWS THAT MATTER: RACE AND OPINIONS ON CLIMATE CHANGE
OF BOSTON AREA RESIDENTS
================================================================================
A growing body of research finds that climate change places a disproportionate
burden on communities of color in the United States. In spite of this evidence,
important discussions taking place about climate change — such as how it is
experienced, which policy solutions are most critical and how we can prepare for
and adapt to its impacts — often leave out the voices of the very communities
most affected.
The Views that Matter report attempts to address that gap by surveying the views
of climate change across racial groups in the Boston area and intentionally

HEAR FROM THE AUTHORS:
"I think it is incredibly important for our voices to be in the table. Most of
the local and national studies on climate change done to date have only been
including the voices and the experiences of the white population."
— Lorna Rivera, Mauricio Gaston Institute for Latino Community
"We hear a lot of speculation about what communities of color might or might not
think about climate change, but we thought it was important to actually ask them."
— Rosalyn Negron, Associate Professor of Anthropology
"We need data that reflects everyone in society, especially significant and
long-silenced communities, if we want equitable climate change policies and
responses."
— J. Cedric Woods, Institute for New England Native American Studies
KEY FINDINGS:
- Residents of color are more likely than white residents to believe that
climate change is happening in Massachusetts (8 in 10) and is a very
serious threat.
- White respondents are the least inclined to view climate change impacts as
affecting some people more than others.
- Respondents, regardless of race, overwhelmingly agree that combatting
climate change requires "major" steps at the federal and state levels.

WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.

CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY

SLIDE 5 — CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================
The first of UMass Boston's Campus Goals for the academic year 2020-21 is to
make UMass Boston a leading anti-racist, health promoting public research
university with excellence at its core. SSL's core values align with this goal.
The below definitions are key to understanding our work:
CLIMATE CHANGE
A shift in average global weather patterns due to increased greenhouse gas
emissions in the atmosphere. It disproportionately impacts low-income
communities and communities of color.
SYSTEMIC RACISM
Among other injustices, systemic racism causes these communities to suffer
more pollution, failing infrastructure, and increased exposure to climate risks.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION
Focused on better protecting people, homes and communities from the impacts
of the climate crisis.
CLIMATE JUSTICE
Climate action that recognizes past injustices and moves us closer to a world
where everyone can thrive despite a changing climate.
================================================================================

WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

SLIDE 3 — DIRECTOR'S MESSAGE
================================================================================
2020 strengthened our resolve to pursue climate justice.
The disproportionate impacts of Covid-19, the increased awakening around racial
justice and the near constant barrage of climate disasters made it clear that
SSL's work is essential and that there are many opportunities for us to lead.
I have been buoyed by how much the national conversation has changed around
climate change and systemic racism over the last year. The Sustainable Solutions
Lab is working to ensure that our climate adaptation efforts take into account
historic marginalization and the disproportionate impact on vulnerable communities.
The climate justice research we are doing, along with showing up for our faculty
of color and community partners, are critical for dismantling white supremacy in
climate adaptation work.
We will secure a safe and healthy future for everyone in the face of the climate
crisis.
With hope,
Rebecca Herst
Director, Sustainable Solutions Lab
================================================================================

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY

SLIDE 5 — CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================
The first of UMass Boston's Campus Goals for the academic year 2020-21 is to
make UMass Boston a leading anti-racist, health promoting public research
university with excellence at its core. SSL's core values align with this goal.
The below definitions are key to understanding our work:
CLIMATE CHANGE
A shift in average global weather patterns due to increased greenhouse gas
emissions in the atmosphere. It disproportionately impacts low-income
communities and communities of color.
SYSTEMIC RACISM
Among other injustices, systemic racism causes these communities to suffer
more pollution, failing infrastructure, and increased exposure to climate risks.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION
Focused on better protecting people, homes and communities from the impacts
of the climate crisis.
CLIMATE JUSTICE
Climate action that recognizes past injustices and moves us closer to a world
where everyone can thrive despite a changing climate.
================================================================================

================================================================================
SSL CLIMATE JUSTICE SEED GRANTS FOR FACULTY
In 2020, SSL launched a Seed Grant Program to incentivize interdisciplinary
climate justice research. This initiative is part of a broader goal to foster
scholarship that examines the impact of climate change on those most vulnerable
to systemic inequities. Each Seed Grant award is for $7,500.
PROJECT: Leave the Trees: Culture, Climate Justice, and Black Diasporas in Boston
Professor Quito Swan and assistant professor Layla D. Brown-Vincent of the
Africana Studies department in the College of Liberal Arts are using their SSL
Seed Grant to explore how the Black Diaspora has engaged in climate justice
through a pop culture lens. The aim of the "Leave the Trees" project is to
generate an archive of discourse and experience that can support the development
of sustainable solutions for the Black community. Additionally, they will map
contemporary Black climate justice activists and organizations in the Boston area.

PROJECT: Climate Justice and the Power of Knowledge in Gloucester's Fishing
Industry
Over the last fifty years, federal and state policies driven by environmental
factors have profoundly affected the fishing industry of Gloucester,
Massachusetts. Assistant professors Antonio Raciti and Alan Wiig and associate
professor Rosalyn Negron of the School for the Environment are applying their SSL
Seed Grant funds to a project that integrates three disciplines (anthropology,
geography and planning) to examine how climate justice is perceived by the fishing
industry and the community. The research team is evaluating the impact of
stakeholders in the fishing industry having different understandings of what
climate justice means. The main goal is to identify a path that takes those varied
climate justice philosophies and transforms them into a shared vision of what
equitable decision-making looks like in the face of climate change.

CLIMATE JUSTICE PARTNERSHIPS

SLIDE 40 — CLIMATE JUSTICE PARTNERSHIPS
================================================================================
In spring 2021, we held a four-part lunch and learn series that explored
successful climate justice partnerships. We hosted representatives from Rebuild
by Design, Good Old Lower East Side, Climate Ready Boston, Catalyst Miami,
Florida International University, the Boston Public Health Commission, Little
Village Environmental Justice Organization, CNT, GreenRoots, Boston University
School of Public Health and The Hyams Foundation. They discussed centering the
needs of communities in the climate adaptation conversation and demonstrated how
researchers and other experts can support climate justice at the local level.

CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE

SLIDE 24 — CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE
================================================================================
Many SSL faculty are relatively new to the field of climate justice. To help them
ground their own scholarship in the academic conversation, Rosalyn Negron and
graduate student Katsyris Rivera-Kientz have created a database of climate justice
research articles. All research starts with a literature review. Launched in March
2021, this resource (housed in Mendeley) contains over 500 articles in a wide
variety of topics from health to housing to governance. All SSL faculty have
access to it and are able to contribute to it themselves so that it will continue
to evolve as expertise on campus grows. This is a central, living resource for SSL
faculty to begin their exploration of climate justice topics.
"Having access to the climate justice research database has allowed me to very
quickly get up to speed on where the academic conversations are in fields beyond
my own. It's giving me a broader interdisciplinary perspective that is essential
for the directions I want to take my research."
— Antonio Raciti, Assistant Professor of Ecological Design, School for the Environment
================================================================================

SHAPING THE CONVERSATION

SLIDE 36 — SHAPING THE CONVERSATION
================================================================================
We are always thinking of what big questions need to be answered and what
conversations need to happen to move the climate justice field forward. To have
the deep impact we aspire to, SSL connects with diverse groups of people to
support their work and inform their decision-making related to climate challenges.
Some highlights include events and thought leadership. Our profile as a leader in
the emerging climate adaptation field is growing. As we continue to engage at the
local, state and international level, our core team and affiliated faculty have
received several awards and grants.

SLIDE 27 — SEED GRANT WINNER
================================================================================
SSL CLIMATE JUSTICE SEED GRANTS FOR FACULTY
In 2020, SSL launched a Seed Grant Program to incentivize interdisciplinary
climate justice research. This initiative is part of a broader goal to foster
scholarship that examines the impact of climate change on those most vulnerable
to systemic inequities. Each Seed Grant award is for $7,500.
PROJECT: Leave the Trees: Culture, Climate Justice, and Black Diasporas in Boston
Professor Quito Swan and assistant professor Layla D. Brown-Vincent of the
Africana Studies department in the College of Liberal Arts are using their SSL
Seed Grant to explore how the Black Diaspora has engaged in climate justice
through a pop culture lens. The aim of the "Leave the Trees" project is to
generate an archive of discourse and experience that can support the development
of sustainable solutions for the Black community. Additionally, they will map
contemporary Black climate justice activists and organizations in the Boston area.
Quito Swan — Professor of Africana Studies, College of Liberal Arts
Layla D. Brown-Vincent — Assistant Professor of Africana Studies, College of Liberal Arts
Deborah Dauda — PhD Candidate, School for Global Inclusion and Social Development
================================================================================

DIRECTOR'S MESSAGE

SLIDE 3 — DIRECTOR'S MESSAGE
================================================================================
2020 strengthened our resolve to pursue climate justice.
The disproportionate impacts of Covid-19, the increased awakening around racial
justice and the near constant barrage of climate disasters made it clear that
SSL's work is essential and that there are many opportunities for us to lead.
I have been buoyed by how much the national conversation has changed around
climate change and systemic racism over the last year. The Sustainable Solutions
Lab is working to ensure that our climate adaptation efforts take into account
historic marginalization and the disproportionate impact on vulnerable communities.
The climate justice research we are doing, along with showing up for our faculty
of color and community partners, are critical for dismantling white supremacy in
climate adaptation work.
We will secure a safe and healthy future for everyone in the face of the climate
crisis.
With hope,
Rebecca Herst
Director, Sustainable Solutions Lab
================================================================================

SLIDE 25 — RESEARCH GRANT WINNER
================================================================================
SSL CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH GRANTS FOR FACULTY
In 2021, SSL awarded two research grants to support faculty conducting research
focused on climate justice. These grants, for up to $50,000, were open to
interdisciplinary teams of tenure or non-tenure track faculty members affiliated
with the colleges, schools and institutes that make up SSL.
PROJECT: Novel Research in Climate Justice: Including Transient Populations
in Climate Resiliency
School for Environment (SFE) associate dean Ellen Douglas, assistant professor
Evan Stewart from the College of Liberal Arts and SFE PhD candidate Johnna
Flahive are using their $48,000 Research Grant for a project that will
characterize the current status and vulnerability of transient populations
(homeless citizens and seasonal international visa workers) within the context
of climate-related risks, focusing on Boston and Cape Cod, Massachusetts. There
are many climate resiliency efforts underway in Massachusetts; however, all
efforts to date have seemingly overlooked transient populations. Their aim is to
identify historical barriers to and future opportunities for involving transient
populations in climate resilience planning and policies.
Ellen Douglas — Associate Dean, Professor of Hydrology, School for the Environment

SLIDE 10 — RESEARCH
================================================================================
Without climate justice research designed and conducted in partnership with
marginalized communities, adaptation efforts may exacerbate existing inequities
and negatively impact society's resilience as a whole.
SSL is stitching these previously siloed areas of expertise into an
interdisciplinary approach and fostering new relationships across fields in order
to better address these extremely complex and interconnected challenges and
catalyze change.
================================================================================

important discussions taking place about climate change — such as how it is
experienced, which policy solutions are most critical and how we can prepare for
and adapt to its impacts — often leave out the voices of the very communities
most affected.

leverage areas of strength within our team and partner networks.

provide testing grounds for building the Decision Support Hub and advancing the study of individual and collective decision-making.

Cape Cod Rail Resilience Project
The Sustainable Solutions Lab (SSL) is proud to be part of the Cape Cod Rail Resilience Project, led by Carlos Velásquez, a PhD candidate at UMass Boston and project manager at MassDOT.
This initiative aims to improve rail safety and climate resilience along the Cape Main Line by integrating advanced technology with stakeholder-driven research methods. The project, inspired by Velásquez’s doctoral research, addresses the increasing risks posed by climate change to critical transportation infrastructure. It was launched in response to a significant 300-foot rail embankment collapse in East Sandwich in 2020, an event linked to climate change-induced drought conditions. With USDOT funding, the team is using drones for mapping and sensors for monitoring water levels. This collaborative effort brings together MassDOT, UMass Boston, and AECOM experts. The innovative approach combines aerial surveys, hydrological drought analysis, and real-time monitoring systems at three pilot study sites.

Bio: I am a postdoctoral researcher at the Centre for European Studies and Comparative Politics (CEE) at Sciences Po Paris, funded by the Bruno Latour Fund. Bio: My work aims to achieve whole-community resilience by moving past individual, fragmented, and incremental efforts and toward holistic, transdisciplinary, systems approaches to climate resilience. Cape Cod Rail Resilience Project
The Sustainable Solutions Lab (SSL) is proud to be part of the Cape Cod Rail Resilience Project, led by Carlos Velásquez, a PhD candidate at UMass Boston and project manager at MassDOT.
This initiative aims to improve rail safety and climate resilience along the Cape Main Line by integrating advanced technology with stakeholder-driven research methods. The project, inspired by Velásquez’s doctoral research, addresses the increasing risks posed by climate change to critical transportation infrastructure. It was launched in response to a significant 300-foot rail embankment collapse in East Sandwich in 2020, an event linked to climate change-induced drought conditions. With USDOT funding, the team is using drones for mapping and sensors for monitoring water levels. This collaborative effort brings together MassDOT, UMass Boston, and AECOM experts. The innovative approach combines aerial surveys, hydrological drought analysis, and real-time monitoring systems at three pilot study sites.

Launched in the Spring of 2022, the Northeast Climate Justice Research Collaborative (The Collaborative) is a trans-disciplinary network for academic and community researchers in the Northeast.

The Collaborative is composed of researchers—whether experienced or just getting started—who are interested in actively working to advance practices and policies that ensure historically excluded communities are safe and healthy despite the changing climate. Through networking, dialogue, funding, and resource-sharing, we support scholars to maximize the benefits of research for the communities they are working with. The Collaborative is convened by the Sustainable Solutions Lab (SSL) at UMass Boston.

Tim has a Bachelor's degree in economics and public policy from Stonehill College and a Master of Public Administration from the McCormack Graduate School at UMass Boston.

WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO

SLIDE 4 — WHO WE ARE / WHAT WE DO
================================================================================
WHO WE ARE:
The Sustainable Solutions Lab or SSL (ess-el) at UMass Boston is an applied
research and action institute working at the intersection of climate and equity.
We are a groundbreaking, cross-disciplinary partnership of five schools and four
institutes across the University:
- Collaborative of Asian American, Native American, Latino, and African
American Institutes (CANALA)
- College of Liberal Arts
- College of Management
- College of Nursing and Health Sciences
- John W. McCormack Graduate School of Policy and Global Studies
- School for the Environment
WHAT WE DO:
Boston has the greatest racial wealth inequality in the U.S. and is the 8th most
vulnerable city to sea-level rise globally.
As part of Boston's only public research university, SSL's mission is to:
1) Understand the disproportionate impacts of climate change on marginalized
communities
2) Partner with them to develop equitable and sustainable solutions.
================================================================================

CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE

SLIDE 24 — CLIMATE JUSTICE RESEARCH DATABASE
================================================================================
Many SSL faculty are relatively new to the field of climate justice. To help them
ground their own scholarship in the academic conversation, Rosalyn Negron and
graduate student Katsyris Rivera-Kientz have created a database of climate justice
research articles. All research starts with a literature review. Launched in March
2021, this resource (housed in Mendeley) contains over 500 articles in a wide
variety of topics from health to housing to governance. All SSL faculty have
access to it and are able to contribute to it themselves so that it will continue
to evolve as expertise on campus grows. This is a central, living resource for SSL
faculty to begin their exploration of climate justice topics.
"Having access to the climate justice research database has allowed me to very
quickly get up to speed on where the academic conversations are in fields beyond
my own. It's giving me a broader interdisciplinary perspective that is essential
for the directions I want to take my research."
— Antonio Raciti, Assistant Professor of Ecological Design, School for the Environment
================================================================================

CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY

SLIDE 5 — CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================
The first of UMass Boston's Campus Goals for the academic year 2020-21 is to
make UMass Boston a leading anti-racist, health promoting public research
university with excellence at its core. SSL's core values align with this goal.
The below definitions are key to understanding our work:
CLIMATE CHANGE
A shift in average global weather patterns due to increased greenhouse gas
emissions in the atmosphere. It disproportionately impacts low-income
communities and communities of color.
SYSTEMIC RACISM
Among other injustices, systemic racism causes these communities to suffer
more pollution, failing infrastructure, and increased exposure to climate risks.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION
Focused on better protecting people, homes and communities from the impacts
of the climate crisis.
CLIMATE JUSTICE
Climate action that recognizes past injustices and moves us closer to a world
where everyone can thrive despite a changing climate.
================================================================================

centering Racial Justice in our work and support our efforts to be an anti-racist
research institute at UMB. As part of this effort, SSL provided Summer
Anti-Racism Research Funding to seven projects led by affiliated faculty with
grants of up to $2,500 for climate justice research that do at least one of

- Propose anti-racist policy changes to address climate disparities
- Center BIPOC voices in the research efforts

most affected.

SLIDES 16-17 — STACY VANDEVEER
================================================================================
LEARNING FROM THE MASSACHUSETTS MUNICIPAL VULNERABILITY PREPAREDNESS (MVP)
PROGRAM IN THE GREATER BOSTON REGION
Research Team: Stacy D. VanDeveer (principal investigator), Patricia Bailey,
David Sulewski
Findings from the Basic Municipal Vulnerability Assessment for Climate Change
Adaptation in the Greater Boston Metropolitan Area. The objective of this study
is to understand conditions in and across municipalities. In 2020, over 80% of
Massachusetts cities and towns had participated in the MVP program and the

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) awarded Lorena Estrada-Martinez,
assistant professor of environment and public health in the School for the
Environment, a three-year grant of $800,000 to study health risks in Vieques,
Puerto Rico. As a result of contamination created by decades of U.S. military
occupation (including the use of chemical and biological weapons), the ecological
and human populations of Vieques have been significantly impacted.
Her study, "Community Driven Assessment of Environmental Health Risks in Vieques,
Puerto Rico," will be supported by a partnership between her research team and the
local community so that all are equally involved in decision-making and
knowledge-sharing. Her team includes SSL faculty members Bob Chen, interim dean
of the SFE and professor of organic geochemistry; Rosalyn Negron, associate
professor of anthropology in the College of Liberal Arts; and Lorna Rivera,
director of the Mauricio Gaston Institute for Latino Community Development and
Public Policy.

Julie Eaton Ernst
Climate Resilience Practice Leader, HNTB
Julie Eaton Ernst is a licensed professional civil engineer devoted to transforming our built, natural, and social environments to be resilient, sustainable, healthy, and equitable. She specializes in resilient design practices and navigating the intersection of policy and engineered solutions. She has led several award-winning projects that have set the standard for integrating climate projections in the A/E/C industry
. As the Climate Resilience Practice Leader at HNTB, Julie actively supports local and national public sector clients and communities with adapting to their changing environments. She serves as chair of the Climate Change and Air Committee for the Environmental Business Council (EBC) of New England. She has bachelor’s degrees in Political Science (University of Rochester) and Civil Engineering (UMass Lowell) and a master’s degree in Civil Engineering (UMass Lowell)
. Julie has been recognized for her contributions to the industry as the recipient of the 2018 Ascending Leader Award from EBC, the 2022 Young Professional of the Year Award from ACEC Massachusetts, and the 2022 Young Professional of the Year Award from ACEC Nationals. She is a contributing author of “Climate Change and the Built Environment,” published by ACEC in 2022.

SLIDE 27 — SEED GRANT WINNER
================================================================================
SSL CLIMATE JUSTICE SEED GRANTS FOR FACULTY
In 2020, SSL launched a Seed Grant Program to incentivize interdisciplinary
climate justice research. This initiative is part of a broader goal to foster
scholarship that examines the impact of climate change on those most vulnerable
to systemic inequities. Each Seed Grant award is for $7,500.
PROJECT: Leave the Trees: Culture, Climate Justice, and Black Diasporas in Boston
Professor Quito Swan and assistant professor Layla D. Brown-Vincent of the
Africana Studies department in the College of Liberal Arts are using their SSL
Seed Grant to explore how the Black Diaspora has engaged in climate justice
through a pop culture lens. The aim of the "Leave the Trees" project is to
generate an archive of discourse and experience that can support the development
of sustainable solutions for the Black community. Additionally, they will map
contemporary Black climate justice activists and organizations in the Boston area.
Quito Swan — Professor of Africana Studies, College of Liberal Arts
Layla D. Brown-Vincent — Assistant Professor of Africana Studies, College of Liberal Arts
Deborah Dauda — PhD Candidate, School for Global Inclusion and Social Development
================================================================================

SLIDE 36 — SHAPING THE CONVERSATION
================================================================================
We are always thinking of what big questions need to be answered and what
conversations need to happen to move the climate justice field forward. To have
the deep impact we aspire to, SSL connects with diverse groups of people to
support their work and inform their decision-making related to climate challenges.
Some highlights include events and thought leadership. Our profile as a leader in
the emerging climate adaptation field is growing. As we continue to engage at the
local, state and international level, our core team and affiliated faculty have
received several awards and grants.
================================================================================

INVESTING IN FACULTY

SLIDE 18 — INVESTING IN FACULTY
================================================================================
Faculty and students are the foundation of everything SSL does. Through research
funding and professional development, SSL can ensure that those who are best
positioned to bring new approaches and shift the field can do so. SSL's approach
is to support faculty's research and their development as scholars, as they are
essential to generating the evidence and advocacy needed for equitable adaptation.
In support of these goals, we created a semester-long program on climate justice
for faculty, built a climate justice research database and granted research and
seed grants.
================================================================================

================================================================================
Without climate justice research designed and conducted in partnership with
marginalized communities, adaptation efforts may exacerbate existing inequities
and negatively impact society's resilience as a whole.
SSL is stitching these previously siloed areas of expertise into an
interdisciplinary approach and fostering new relationships across fields in order
to better address these extremely complex and interconnected challenges and
catalyze change.

most affected.

CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY

SLIDE 5 — CLIMATE ACTION TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================
The first of UMass Boston's Campus Goals for the academic year 2020-21 is to
make UMass Boston a leading anti-racist, health promoting public research
university with excellence at its core. SSL's core values align with this goal.
The below definitions are key to understanding our work:
CLIMATE CHANGE
A shift in average global weather patterns due to increased greenhouse gas
emissions in the atmosphere. It disproportionately impacts low-income
communities and communities of color.
SYSTEMIC RACISM
Among other injustices, systemic racism causes these communities to suffer
more pollution, failing infrastructure, and increased exposure to climate risks.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION
Focused on better protecting people, homes and communities from the impacts
of the climate crisis.
CLIMATE JUSTICE
Climate action that recognizes past injustices and moves us closer to a world
where everyone can thrive despite a changing climate.
================================================================================
